title: Ibn Arabi's heart
hookLine: Ibn Arabi wrote that his heart had become able to take every form, in his own Sufi sense (Tarjuman al-Ashwaq 11)

lines: A HEART ABLE TO TAKE EVERY FORM.
cards: Water has no shape of its own. Pour it into a cup and it's cup-shaped; into a vase, vase-shaped; into a cupped hand, it fits the hand. Nobody calls the water unfaithful for that.
A Muslim mystic named Ibn Arabi, writing in Arabic, said something like that about his own heart. In a book of love poems, he wrote that his heart had become able to take every form.

teach.b: The collection is called the Interpreter of Desires. Ibn Arabi writes, in paraphrase: my heart has become able to take every form.

It is a pasture for gazelles, a cloister for monks, a temple for idols, the Kaaba of the pilgrim, the tablets of the Torah and the book of the Quran. Then: I follow the religion of love, wherever its camels turn.

teach.h: A LOVE POEM AND ITS COMMENTARY.
teach.b: Around it is a love poem, full of longing for a beloved, ruined campsites and departing caravans, the old images of Arabic love poetry.

Tradition says some readers objected that the poems were simply worldly love songs, and Ibn Arabi answered by writing a commentary on them, reading each image as a sign of divine knowledge. Readers hear the poem two ways.
Some hear it saying every religion is the same.
Others hear something narrower and stranger: a Muslim heart so turned toward God that it can recognize God's self-disclosure wherever it appears. This lesson doesn't choose between them.
Either way, the image is a heart that doesn't harden into one shape against the world. It stays able to receive. Like water, it takes the form of what it meets, and stays water.

how: Ibn Arabi's writings are studied in Sufi circles and universities alike, and this poem from the Tarjuman al-Ashwaq is often read together with his own commentary on it.

o: an Arab king who built a temple for every faith
a Muslim mystic whose heart could take every form
a Persian poet who told of love as an astrolabe

games.q: inside the poem — tap the pairs.

s: Ibn Arabi wrote this as a love poem
it sits in a collection full of longing for a beloved, which he later read as divine knowledge.
all readers agree the poem says every religion is the same
some read it that way; others hear a Muslim heart recognizing God wherever God appears.
the heart in the poem hardens into one shape
it becomes able to take every form, like water.

games.q: readers object that your love poems are just worldly love songs. you're Ibn Arabi. what do you do?
o: write a commentary reading each image as divine knowledge.
games.why: tradition says he answered by writing a commentary on his own poems, reading their images as signs of knowledge of God.

practice: Bring to mind a person or a place where you usually close up a little, a relative who talks politics, a neighborhood you avoid, a coworker who rubs you the wrong way, and notice what happens in your chest.

Without agreeing or approving, picture your heart as water meeting that shape: it doesn't have to become them, it just doesn't have to turn to stone. If you pray, you can hold that person in your own tradition's words.

wordCard.voice: Ibn Arabi. The Muslim mystic who wrote that his heart had become able to take every form, a pasture, a cloister, a temple, a Kaaba. Today's word.

orig.note: Arabic: heart, the word in the poem's opening line about taking every form.

carryVoice: Your line: able to take every form. A heart can stay open without losing itself. Until tomorrow.

sources.work: Ibn Arabi, Tarjuman al-Ashwaq (The Interpreter of Desires)
